chapter: INTRO: WHERE DECISIONS ACTUALLY HAPPEN (3 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Episode one, we said it almost in passing: decisions of consequence are almost never made in the room where they're announced. Today we stop saying it in passing and make it the whole episode. Because once you accept that sentence, a question opens up underneath it that most executives never systematically answer: if the decision isn't made in the meeting, where is it made, and what does deliberately working that place look like? The answer is coalitions, and the discipline of building them. And I want to defuse the flinch right away, because I can hear it — "coalition" sounds like politics, and politics is what the bad people do.
chapter: INTRO: WHERE DECISIONS ACTUALLY HAPPEN (3 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Here's the defusal, and it's the same one from episode one: the test is whether it survives discovery. A coalition built by trading favors for votes on something you privately know is weak — that's corrosion, and it eventually surfaces and takes you with it. A coalition built by getting the right people genuinely bought into a good idea, in the right order, with their fingerprints legitimately on it — that's just how organizations decide. It has always been how organizations decide. The executives who call coalition-building "politics" and refuse it aren't being pure. They're outsourcing the coalition to chance, and then losing to whoever didn't. <breath> And there's a second reason this episode matters: the day comes for everyone when the obstacle isn't a skeptical room. It's one specific person with real power who has decided your initiative doesn't happen. The blocker. We'll spend a full segment on them.
chapter: INTRO: WHERE DECISIONS ACTUALLY HAPPEN (3 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Three tools today. Coalition mechanics — the minimum winning coalition and who to recruit first, which is not who you think. Sequencing — why the order of conversations changes the outcome, and the craft of engineered co-authorship. And the blocker playbook — diagnosis before combat, and escalation as the last tool that doesn't have to end the relationship. Scenario at the end, and it's a hard one: post-acquisition platform consolidation, blocked by a beloved founder-GM with board relationships.
chapter: INTRO: WHERE DECISIONS ACTUALLY HAPPEN (3 minutes)

text: [MUSIC FADES]
chapter: INTRO: WHERE DECISIONS ACTUALLY HAPPEN (3 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Tool one. Start with the mental shift, because it reframes everything downstream: stop preparing for meetings and start designing sequences. The big meeting — the exec review, the investment committee — is not where minds change. It's where positions that already exist get performed and ratified. By the time the meeting starts, the outcome is usually the arithmetic of commitments people walked in carrying. So the unit of work is not the deck. The unit of work is the series of one-on-one conversations that determine what people carry in. The meeting before the meeting isn't a cynical add-on to the process. It is the process. The meeting is the receipt.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: COALITION MECHANICS (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: And once you see it that way, you can borrow a beautifully cold idea from political science — Riker's minimum winning coalition. You do not need everyone. You need the smallest set of people whose combined weight makes your outcome the default — and "weight" here is the power column from your episode-one map, in all four denominations: formal authority, budget, veto-by-expertise, and social permission. Count who actually tips this specific decision. It's usually two to four people, and — this is the part that saves you a month — it's usually not the whole room. Executives burn entire quarters evangelizing the persuadable middle because persuading the friendly feels productive. The map says most of those conversations were never load-bearing.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: COALITION MECHANICS (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Which sets up the most counterintuitive rule in the episode: recruit the skeptic-with-standing first. Not your allies. The instinct is to start warm — collect the easy yeses, build momentum, feel good. But think about what a yes actually carries, informationally. Episode four said a yes from someone who always says yes carries zero information. Same physics here: five allies nodding tells the room nothing — of course your friends agree with you. But the one person known for shredding weak proposals, standing next to yours? That's evidence. Their conversion does persuasion you can't do for yourself, because their credibility isn't correlated with your interest. One converted skeptic with standing is worth five cheerful allies, and it isn't close.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: COALITION MECHANICS (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: There's a second, less obvious return on going to the skeptic first: their objections arrive while the proposal is still cheap to change. This is your red team, working for free. If the idea has a real flaw, you want it found in a one-on-one in week two, not performed in the exec review in week nine. And notice the compounding move — when you go back to the skeptic and say "you were right about the migration risk, here's how the plan changed," you've done three things at once: improved the plan, paid them the recognition currency, and converted their objection into ownership, because the plan now contains their thinking. Skeptics who see their fingerprints in version three defend version three.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: COALITION MECHANICS (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: One more distinction and it's load-bearing for the whole hour: alignment is not agreement. A functioning coalition is not everyone enthusiastic. It's your minimum winning set genuinely committed, a few skeptics moved to "I wouldn't choose this, but I can live with it and I won't fight it" — and that's a complete victory, stop pushing past it. Executives lose won games by trying to convert lived-with into loved. You need consent to proceed, not consensus of the heart. Chasing the second after you have the first doesn't just waste time — it reopens questions that had settled, and spends currency you'll want later.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: COALITION MECHANICS (6 minutes)

chapter: SEGMENT 1: COALITION MECHANICS (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Tool two. So you know your minimum winning coalition. The next question sounds trivial and decides outcomes: in what order do you have the conversations? Because order isn't logistics. Order is strategy, for one deep reason — every early conversation happens while the idea is still soft, and every late conversation happens after it's hardened. The people you see early get to shape the thing; the people you see late get to react to it. So the sequence is really an allocation decision: whose thinking gets baked into the foundation, and who receives a finished object. Allocate badly and you've turned a would-be co-author into a critic — same person, same idea, different week.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: SEQUENCING AND ENGINEERED CO-AUTHORSHIP (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Which is why the phrase I want everyone to steal from this episode is wet concrete. Go to the people whose support you most need while the concrete is still wet — explicitly, visibly unfinished. "I'm working through something and I want your read before this goes anywhere" is one of the most disarming sentences in organizational life, and almost nobody senior uses it, because showing unfinished work feels like showing weakness. It's the opposite. A polished deck triggers evaluation mode — arms folded, find the flaw. A rough sketch triggers contribution mode — leaning in, co-solving. And contribution converts to ownership on contact: people defend what they helped build with an energy no persuasion can rent. Cohen and Bradford would call it paying the respect currency. I'd call it the cheapest equity you'll ever issue.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: SEQUENCING AND ENGINEERED CO-AUTHORSHIP (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: And say the quiet mechanism out loud — engineered co-authorship. Yes, engineered: you are deliberately designing whose fingerprints end up on this idea. Deliberately asking the CFO's team to build the cost model with you instead of checking your math afterward. Deliberately leaving a genuinely open question in the design — not a fake one, an open one — for the skeptic-with-standing to answer. And when it's half Priya's idea by the end, you say "this was half Priya's idea," and here's the ethical hinge the whole tool swings on: you have to mean it. Manufactured credit is flattery with paperwork, people smell it in a week, and the trust equation collects with interest. Real co-authorship means you actually let the idea change. The price of their fingerprints is your fingerprints no longer covering everything. Most executives claim they'll pay that price and flinch at the first real amendment. <laugh> The ones who genuinely pay it stop having to sell their ideas at all — the coalition sells it for them, because it's theirs too.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: SEQUENCING AND ENGINEERED CO-AUTHORSHIP (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Now the sequencing heuristics, because order-of-operations is where this gets concrete. First: anyone whose expertise could kill the idea sees it before anyone whose authority could bless it — because when the CEO asks "what does security think," the answer must never be "I haven't asked." Second: the skeptic-with-standing goes early, segment one already made that case. Third — subtle one — think hard about who you deliberately bring in late-middle: sometimes a person's contribution genuinely lands best once the shape exists, and wasting their one fresh read on formless mush spends access currency for nothing. And fourth: the sponsor with formal authority usually goes last-before-the-room, and what you bring them is not a pitch. It's the assembled coalition — "engineering's in, finance built the model with us, Priya's redesigned the rollout." At that point you're not asking them to take a risk. You're offering them a parade to walk in front of.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: SEQUENCING AND ENGINEERED CO-AUTHORSHIP (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: One failure mode before the hard segment, and it's the one that gets sequencing a bad name: running the whole campaign in whispers and letting the eventual room feel it was pre-cooked. People can forgive losing an argument. What they don't forgive is discovering the argument was over before they were told it existed. The fix is disclosure of process, which costs nothing: "I've been working this through with finance and the platform team over the past month; here's where it landed and here's what's still genuinely open." Said plainly, in the room. The campaign survives discovery — because you disclosed it yourself. That's the episode-one test, passed on purpose. <breath> Alright. All of that is the game on normal difficulty. Now the boss level: what happens when one person with real power just says no.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: SEQUENCING AND ENGINEERED CO-AUTHORSHIP (6 minutes)

text: [PAUSE]
chapter: SEGMENT 2: SEQUENCING AND ENGINEERED CO-AUTHORSHIP (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Tool three. First, define the term honestly, because "blocker" is doing a lot of self-serving work in most executives' vocabularies. A blocker is not someone who disagrees with you — that's a skeptic, previous segment, often useful. A blocker is someone with the power column filled in — formal veto, budget control, or enough social permission that their frown freezes everyone else — who has decided your initiative should not happen and is acting on it. And before any playbook: sit with the possibility that the blocker is right. Some of the best decisions in your company's history are initiatives somebody blocked. If you can't state their case so well they'd endorse your summary, you haven't earned the rest of this segment.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: THE BLOCKER PLAYBOOK (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Then diagnosis before combat, because blockers come in three species and the treatments are incompatible. Species one: substantive — they know something, or believe they know something, about why this fails. Treatment: engage the content for real, wet concrete, red team, everything from segment two — substantive blockers are convertible into your strongest co-authors because their conversion has the highest information value in the building. Species two: positional — the objection is what your initiative does to their world: their headcount, their charter, their standing, the story they tell about their org. Watch for the tell — arguments that keep shifting while the conclusion never moves. Rebutting the stated argument does nothing, because the stated argument isn't the objection; this is episode one's currency problem — the initiative as designed makes them pay, so the move is to redesign what it costs them or what it pays them. And species three: historical — the objection is about the last time. The wound. Your predecessor's migration that torched their roadmap, the credit that got taken. The tell here is heat disproportionate to stakes, and it's a trust-equation problem — no amount of present-tense argument will fix it, because the argument isn't in the present tense.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: THE BLOCKER PLAYBOOK (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: The most common diagnostic failure, worth naming because sophisticated people make it: assuming positional or historical because it flatters you. "He's just protecting his turf" is the most comfortable sentence in corporate life — it means you don't have to engage the possibility that he's right. Run the test honestly: ask the calibrated questions from episode two — "what would this have to look like for you to be comfortable?" is diagnostic gold, because substantive blockers answer with conditions, positional blockers answer with fog, and historical blockers answer with the past. And most real blockers are a blend, which means most real treatments are too.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: THE BLOCKER PLAYBOOK (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Now escalation, because sometimes diagnosis and redesign and time all fail, and the initiative matters, and there is a boss you could take it to. Rules of engagement — four of them, learned expensively. One: escalate the decision, never the person. You are asking for a call on a question two reasonable executives couldn't resolve — you are not filing a complaint. The paper you bring says "here are two positions and their costs; we need a decision," and it states their position at full strength, so faithfully they'd sign it. Two: never surprise them — this is episode four's contract applied sideways. The move that preserves the relationship is telling them first, plainly: "we're stuck, I think it needs a decision above us — I'd rather we bring it together; will you?" Sometimes that sentence alone unsticks it, because it converts the fight into a shared problem. Three: accept the verdict completely, in both directions — if you lose, you lose all the way, episode four rules, no appeal-by-hallway. And four: price it honestly before you start. Escalation is expensive even when you win — you've demonstrated you couldn't resolve a peer conflict laterally, and the boss noticed. Twice a year is a leadership pattern. More is your pattern.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: THE BLOCKER PLAYBOOK (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: And hold on to the reframe hiding in the diagnosis, because it's the segment's real gift: a substantive blocker engaged early isn't an obstacle at all. They're the best red team you'll ever get for free, plus — episode-one arithmetic — the highest-value coalition member available, precisely because everyone knows they can't be bought. The executives who treat every blocker as an enemy fight wars they didn't need to fight. The ones who diagnose first end up with the strange, valuable thing: a former blocker in the front row. <breath> Which is exactly the ending we're going to try to engineer in the scenario, and I promise it will not go smoothly.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: THE BLOCKER PLAYBOOK (5 minutes)

text: [MUSIC STING]
chapter: SEGMENT 3: THE BLOCKER PLAYBOOK (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: The setup. You're the CPO of a company that eighteen months ago acquired a smaller competitor — call it Meridian — largely for its customers and its team. You now run two overlapping platforms: two billing systems, two data pipelines, duplicated infrastructure burning roughly a fifth of total engineering capacity just keeping both alive. Consolidation is obviously right; everyone technical agrees in private. The blocker is Marcus: Meridian's founder, now a GM running his old company as a business unit. Beloved by his people — half of whom have follow-him-out-the-door loyalty. Two board members came with the acquisition and adore him. And the consolidation plan, as drafted, migrates Meridian's customers onto your stack and dissolves most of what makes his unit his. He's said no — gracefully, repeatedly, immovably. Your team wants you to escalate to the CEO. You have the votes, they say. Probably true. <laugh> Let's count what winning that way costs.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- THE FOUNDER WHO SAYS NO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Price it out, because the arithmetic kills the shortcut: you escalate, you win, and Monday morning Marcus is running the unit whose migration he opposed, in front of engineers watching how the acquirer treats their founder, with two board members hearing his version at dinner first. The initiative needs eighteen months of his people's goodwill to actually execute — and you just converted their leader into a conscripted opponent. You'd win the decision and lose the migration. So: playbook from the top. Diagnose. Is Marcus substantive, positional, or historical? Run the calibrated question — "what would consolidation have to look like for you to be comfortable?" — and listen hard. Suppose you get back some real technical content: Meridian's biggest customers depend on a data-residency feature your stack handles worse — that's substantive, flag it, that's gold. But underneath it, fog and the past: "we were promised autonomy in the deal" — historical, an actual wound with actual paperwork — and a conclusion that never moves however the arguments shift, because the plan as drafted erases the thing with his name on it. Positional. All three species in one blocker. Which is the normal case.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- THE FOUNDER WHO SAYS NO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Treatment plan, species by species, and notice we haven't touched the org chart yet. Substantive: his data-residency objection goes straight into the plan's foundation — wet concrete — and you go back to him with "you were right, this changed the architecture; the residency layer is now the first milestone." First fingerprints: his. Historical: the wound gets named, out loud, by you, because unspoken it poisons everything — "the deal promised autonomy, and this plan as I first drafted it broke that promise. I want to renegotiate that honestly rather than pretend it isn't happening." You cannot argue a wound away, but you can be the first acquirer-side executive who acknowledges it, and that single act moves more than any deck. And positional — the real one — you redesign what the initiative costs him. As drafted: his platform dies, his org dissolves, his story ends. Redesigned: the merged platform team is led out of Meridian's engineering core — genuinely, they're stronger on data infrastructure, this passes the survives-discovery test — the residency architecture that wins the migration carries his product's DNA and everyone will know it, and his unit's identity re-founds on the customer segment he actually loves, not the duplicated plumbing he privately knows is doomed. You're not paying him off. You're re-denominating the initiative so it stops costing him his story.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- THE FOUNDER WHO SAYS NO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Now the coalition, in sequence. Minimum winning set: the CEO ratifies; the CTO and CFO tip it; the two Meridian board members can veto it socially through the CEO. Fine — but who goes first? Not the CEO. Not the friendly CTO. Marcus. Wet concrete, before anyone else has seen anything, precisely because he's the blocker: "before this goes anywhere near the exec team, I want to build the residency plan with you — and I want to talk about the autonomy promise, because I don't think we've been honest about it." If he engages, everything downstream transforms. Then the sequence writes itself: CTO next — expertise that could kill it, and he pressure-tests the residency-first architecture. CFO third, building the cost model with you — the fifth of engineering capacity, denominated her way; co-authored numbers, episode-one rules. The Meridian board members you don't work around — that's the whisper-campaign failure mode — they hear it from you and Marcus together, or the whole thing dies at a dinner you weren't at. And the CEO, last, receives the parade: architecture Marcus co-designed, model finance built, board members pre-briefed by the two of you jointly. The meeting approves in twenty minutes what eighteen months of escalation memos couldn't touch.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- THE FOUNDER WHO SAYS NO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: And if Marcus still says no? Because sometimes he does, and a playbook that only works on cooperative blockers is a story, not a playbook. Then — and only then — escalation, by the rules: you tell him first, to his face, and you invite him to bring it jointly; the paper states his case at full strength, signed-off-by-him strength; you're asking the CEO to decide a question, not to discipline a founder. You might lose — the board members are real, and episode two taught you to know your BATNA before you sit down: what does engineering-capacity life look like if consolidation waits a year? And if you win, you win having done every honorable thing first, in a way Marcus himself — this matters most — watched happen. The relationship has a scar, not an amputation. But run the diagnosis-first version and you mostly never arrive here. The blocker episode ends the way the good ones do: with the residency milestone shipping early, and Marcus presenting the migration to the board. His slide. His name on it. Genuinely earned.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- THE FOUNDER WHO SAYS NO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Trace it: diagnosis told you the no was three different nos wearing one face. The redesign paid each species in its own currency. The sequence put the blocker's fingerprints first, not last. And the room, when it finally met, was a receipt. Escalation stayed in the holster the whole time — which is exactly where it does its best work.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- THE FOUNDER WHO SAYS NO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Homework, one hour: take the biggest thing you're trying to move this quarter and write the sequence, not the deck. Minimum winning coalition — names, not roles. Who sees it while the concrete's wet. Which skeptic-with-standing goes first. And if you've got a blocker: one honest paragraph diagnosing the species — and the test is whether you could read that paragraph to their face.
